bullet: Pencroff accepts him as one more aboard, relieving the car of two bags of sand (I.2 ¶54). *(Drafted.)*
Nab trusts him to be near his master in the water (I.3 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
Cyrus Smith, fearing excess weight, wanted to send the poor animal away (I.2 ¶53). *(Drafted.)*
He vanishes when the engineer is swept off, having gone of his own will to his master's aid (I.3 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*
The castaways reckon that, if near, Top's barking would reach them should Cyrus be unable to give a sign (I.3 ¶15). *(Drafted.)*
The reporter reports that no trace was found of the engineer or of the dog Top on the coast (I.5 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff, hunting, wishes he had Top, but takes him for lost with his master (I.6 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
He reaches the Chimneys, which he did not know, by instinct, in the night and the storm, and is neither tired, nor exhausted, nor soiled with mud or sand (I.7 ¶64). *(Drafted.)*
At the name of Cyrus Smith he barks softly, as if to say his master was saved (I.7 ¶74). *(Drafted.)*
He leads the way over the dunes without a single hesitation (I.7 ¶82). *(Drafted.)*
In the sea he rushed to his master's help; he held him up by his clothes, and sank with him (I.8 ¶67). *(Drafted.)*
He sleeps at his master's feet (I.9 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*
He seizes the capybara by an ear and follows it into the pond, swimming on the surface to find it (I.9 ¶103). *(Drafted.)*
He leaps on the capybara when it surfaces and stops it diving again (I.9 ¶114). *(Drafted.)*
On Pencroff's offer, he studies the sailor's open face and cannot doubt he is an honest man (I.2 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*
He is not a man to let an occasion slip; he judges Pencroff's plan very dangerous and therefore feasible (I.2 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
He decides they will go, with Spilett and Nab, and names the hour of ten that evening (I.2 ¶41). *(Drafted.)*
He slips onto the square at half past nine with his companions (I.2 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
He gives the order of departure (I.2 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
He wants to send Top away for fear of excess weight (I.2 ¶53). *(Drafted.)*
He cannot think of descending during the night of the departure; five days later a clearing shows the sea beneath the balloon (I.2 ¶56). *(Drafted.)*
He is carried off by a sea through the torn meshes of the netting when the balloon falls on the coast; Top has vanished too (I.3 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff says that if they ever saw him again he would know how to turn the maze of the Chimneys to account (I.4 ¶25). *(Drafted.)*
On 25 March the reporter and Nab, having found no trace of him along eight miles of coast, take him for drowned (I.5 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
Nab refuses to believe him dead, calling him a man to come back from anything (I.5 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
Nab says that if he were there he would know how to make a fire (I.5 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
His first intelligible words, half conscious, are "Île ou continent ?" (I.8 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He concludes that he must have walked like a sleepwalker, Top leading him after pulling him from the waves (I.8 ¶80). *(Drafted.)*
He thinks it likely that they lie on a land of the Pacific, the balloon having covered six to seven thousand miles (I.9 ¶70). *(Drafted.)*
Asked by Pencroff where to begin, he answers that they begin at the beginning (I.13 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*
He says the first need is a kiln, to make pottery (I.13 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
He decides to set the workshop at the clay itself, to avoid carrying (I.13 ¶16). *(Drafted.)*
Wishing for a knife, he speaks as if to himself (I.13 ¶21). *(Drafted.)*
His look brightens when it falls on Top (I.13 ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
He breaks Top's collar in two and calls the halves two knives (I.13 ¶26). *(Drafted.)*
He leads the party back to the clay he had noticed on the lake's western shore (I.13 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*
He makes the bricks by hand, without moulds (I.13 ¶32). *(Drafted.)*
On 2 April he sets about fixing the island's orientation (I.13 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He takes the sun's meridian passage from the noted times of sunset and sunrise, and sets two trees in line with it as a fixed meridian (I.13 ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
He warns the hunters to be extremely prudent, since large clawed animals have passed (I.13 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
He guides Nab and Pencroff in carrying limestone, which gives quicklime and, with sand, mortar (I.13 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He had found an open-air coal seam near the mouth of Red Creek (I.13 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
He has a little lime and quartz added to the clay for the pottery (I.13 ¶47). *(Drafted.)*
He will turn the colonists into smiths whenever he sees fit (I.13 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
He finds a plant of the wormwood genus that can replace tinder (I.13 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Pencroff it is not tobacco but Chinese mugwort, tinder for them (I.13 ¶55). *(Drafted.)*
He later soaks it in potassium nitrate, of which the island has several beds (I.13 ¶56). *(Drafted.)*
He had saluted the Southern Cross from the summit of Mount Franklin some days earlier (I.13 ¶58). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Harbert that next day true and mean time coincide, and that he may find the island's longitude (I.13 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
He says he will try tonight for the latitude from the height of the Southern Cross, since they need to know the island's distance from the continents and archipelagos (I.13 ¶65). *(Drafted.)*
Without a sextant, he cuts two small flat rules and joins them into a compass, pinned with an acacia thorn (I.13 ¶69). *(Drafted.)*
He chooses the Grande-Vue plateau for the sighting because Cape Claw hides the southern horizon (I.13 ¶70). *(Drafted.)*
He sights the horizon and the star alpha with the two arms and pins the arms to a third board to keep the angle (I.13 ¶76). *(Drafted.)*
On seeing Captain Nemo he says "Je vous connais !" (III.16 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He approaches Nemo's couch (III.16 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He says he knows the name of the submarine apparatus, the Nautilus (III.16 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Nemo that a man who had made no pledge to him, and so cannot be called a traitor, gave the secret away (III.16 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*
He says he has no call to judge Nemo's past life and, like everyone, does not know its motives (III.16 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
He names Nemo as the good, generous, powerful being to whom they owe their lives (III.16 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
He urges Nemo several times to rest (III.16 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
After the life story he recalls all the incidents that helped the colony and thanks Nemo (III.16 ¶67). *(Drafted.)*
He understands Nemo's allusion to the sunk frigate and does not answer (III.16 ¶72). *(Drafted.)*
Asked his view, he says Nemo's error was to believe the past could be revived (III.16 ¶79). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Nemo history will not condemn his name (III.16 ¶79). *(Drafted.)*
He tells Nemo the honest men he helped will mourn him for ever (III.16 ¶83). *(Drafted.)*
He came through his capture, as ever, without a scratch; his last words noted were "Un sudiste me couche en joue et…" (I.2 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff fears he has kept his notebook rather than his box of matches (I.5 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He is sure that Cyrus Smith will find a way to make fire, "with nothing" (I.9 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
A plate is captioned with his name (I.2 pl1). *(Drafted.)*
Committed by Smith's "nous", he approves the plan without reserve and is only surprised he had not thought of it himself (I.2 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
After the fall he cries "En avant !" and leads the search for the engineer (I.3 ¶2). *(Drafted.)*
He says Cyrus's silence proves nothing and that they must not despair (I.3 ¶28). *(Drafted.)*
He proposes lighting a signal fire for the engineer, but there is no wood on the islet (I.3 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*
He agrees with Pencroff to wait for low water and keep together as much as they can (I.3 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
At about ten o'clock on 25 March he crosses the channel with Pencroff and Harbert, clothes bundled on his head (I.3 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*
He goes off up the coast alone on Nab's track, impatient for news of the engineer (I.4 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*
He and Nab searched the coast for more than eight miles and found no trace of the engineer (I.5 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He eats the shellfish, lies down by a rock, exhausted but calm (I.5 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
He says he had matches but must have thrown them all away (I.5 ¶57). *(Drafted.)*
He tears a leaf from his notebook for the fire (I.5 ¶73). *(Drafted.)*
He notes the day's incidents in summary before sleeping (I.5 ¶88). *(Drafted.)*
He finds the double disappearance of Cyrus and Top, living or dead, inexplicable and improbable (I.7 ¶18). *(Drafted.)*
He alone is kept awake by anxiety through the storm, reproaching himself for not having gone with Nab (I.7 ¶34). *(Drafted.)*
Called "le reporter", he asks what happens if food runs short for want of hunting tools (I.13 ¶17). *(Drafted.)*
He and Harbert once saw an animal that looked like a jaguar (I.13 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He promises himself, once he has a serious weapon, to wage war on the wild beasts and purge the island of them (I.13 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He asks whether Cyrus can find the longitude without instruments or sextant (I.13 ¶64). *(Drafted.)*
He says that, if they are within a hundred miles of an inhabited coast, a boat might serve them better than a house (I.13 ¶66). *(Drafted.)*
He takes Nemo's hand and finds it burning (III.16 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
Nemo signs to him and the engineer to sit (III.16 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
He offers Nemo his care, and is told it is useless (III.16 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
He takes his place in the car with the others while Pencroff casts off the ballast (I.2 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
He notes that one of Nab's cries seemed to echo, which suggests a coast to the west (I.3 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
He identifies the shellfish on the rocks as lithodomes, not mussels (I.4 ¶12). *(Drafted.)*
The young naturalist recognises "déodars" among the conifers (I.4 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*
He identifies the birds as wild or rock pigeons by the double black band on the wing, the white rump and the ash-blue plumage (I.4 ¶58). *(Drafted.)*
He sets out to look for a cave in the rocks to shelter in (I.4 ¶6). *(Drafted.)*
He says that when Smith returns he must find a tolerable dwelling (I.4 ¶26). *(Drafted.)*
He believes so energetic a man as Smith cannot have let himself drown (I.4 ¶43). *(Drafted.)*
He suggests lighting a fire as savages do, by rubbing two dry sticks together (I.5 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He offers Nab shellfish and begs him to eat (I.5 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
He deftly draws the single match from the waistcoat lining without breaking it (I.5 ¶68). *(Drafted.)*
At Pencroff's trembling refusal he strikes the match on a pebble and lights the fire; never had he been so moved (I.5 ¶78). *(Drafted.)*
He finds salt left in the hollows of the rocks by evaporation (I.6 ¶10). *(Drafted.)*
He suggests burnt linen as a substitute for tinder (I.6 ¶15). *(Drafted.)*
He names a bird of the marshy forest as a "jacamar" (I.6 ¶22). *(Drafted.)*
He throws a stone skilfully and hard at the jacamar and strikes it at the wing root, but not hard enough to stop it (I.6 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*
He names the little long-tailed birds as couroucous from their shed feathers (I.6 ¶29). *(Drafted.)*
He knows that couroucous are good to eat, their flesh very delicate, and easy to club (I.6 ¶31). *(Drafted.)*
He recognises the male tétras by the two pointed wing-tufts (I.6 ¶37). *(Drafted.)*
It is the first time he has seen birds taken on a line (I.6 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
He reasons that whatever is new in Nab's long absence can only be to Cyrus Smith's advantage (I.7 ¶22). *(Drafted.)*
He gathers edible seaweed (a sargasso of the fucaceae) from high rocks that the sea wets only at spring tides (I.9 ¶18). *(Drafted.)*
He finds a tree with edible fruit, the pine nut tree, whose almonds are ripe (I.9 ¶97). *(Drafted.)*
He takes the animal Top holds for a capybara, one of the largest of the rodents (I.9 ¶104). *(Drafted.)*
He knows the capybara has webbed feet and is almost an amphibian (I.9 ¶112). *(Drafted.)*
He discovers on the way the tree whose branches the South American Indians use for bows, the "crejimba", a palm that bears no edible fruit (I.13 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
He and Pencroff had chased a jacamar on their first expedition (I.13 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
He and the reporter become very skilful archers (I.13 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
He and Gédéon Spilett see a jaguar-like animal that does not attack them (I.13 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He confirms to Cyrus Smith that it is 15 April (I.13 ¶62). *(Drafted.)*
He stands aside with the others in Nemo's salon (III.16 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He draws near to Nemo, kneels, takes his hand and kisses it (III.16 ¶84). *(Drafted.)*
Nemo, with a tear, calls him "mon enfant" and blesses him (III.16 ¶86). *(Drafted.)*
His departure, fixed for 18 March by night, is put off because the north-west wind turns to a hurricane (I.2 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*
Neither he nor his companions can think of braving the hurricane in the frail car (I.2 ¶46). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
He follows his master wherever his master wishes to go (I.2 ¶42). *(Drafted.)*
He weeps with rage and despair at having lost all he loved in the world (I.3 ¶4). *(Drafted.)*
He says his master can swim (I.3 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
On the morning of 25 March he plunges into the current without a word, in haste to reach the coast and go north (I.3 ¶43). *(Drafted.)*
He swims the half-mile channel obliquely in more than half an hour, drifting fast, and lands several thousand feet from where he started (I.3 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
On returning at about six he has red eyes from weeping and has lost all hope (I.5 ¶41). *(Drafted.)*
He cries out that his master is not dead (I.5 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He refuses food: deprived of his master he can no longer, or will no longer, live (I.5 ¶50). *(Drafted.)*
He is the one castaway who does not rest in the Chimneys; he wanders the shore all night calling his master (I.5 ¶90). *(Drafted.)*
On the morning of 26 March he goes back north along the coast, to where the sea had closed over Smith (I.6 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
He finds footprints in the sand toward five in the evening, on the day he left the Chimneys at dawn (26 March, by I.6 ¶9) (I.8 ¶21). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
He follows the footprints a quarter of a mile toward the dunes, careful not to efface them, and Top leads him to his master (I.8 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
Cyrus Smith says Nab will bring provisions to the brickyard (I.13 ¶16). *(Drafted.)*
He and Pencroff, guided by Cyrus Smith, haul loads of limestone on a hurdle of woven branches (I.13 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He prepares a pot-au-feu of agouti and flavoured capybara ham for the evening meal at the Chimneys (I.13 ¶57). *(Drafted.)*
He stands aside with the others in Nemo's salon (III.16 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He and Pencroff had expected to find almost a god in the "génie de l’île" (III.16 ¶10). *(Drafted.)*
He accosts Cyrus Smith in a Richmond street and asks whether he has had enough of Richmond (I.2 ¶25). *(Drafted.)*
He proposes escape by the idle balloon, which seems to be waiting for them (I.2 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
In the storm he says it is a nasty tide but they will get through (I.2 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
At the balloon he detaches the ballast bags on Smith's order (I.2 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
He welcomes Top aboard ("un de plus"), lightening the car by two bags of sand, and casts off the rope (I.2 ¶54). *(Drafted.)*
He asks whether the lost engineer can swim (I.3 ¶10). *(Drafted.)*
In the dark he thinks he recognises gulls and mews among the birds (I.3 ¶14). *(Drafted.)*
He sees that they are on an islet, not the mainland (I.3 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*
He says he feels the coast though he cannot see it (I.3 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He holds Spilett back from the channel, judging the current an ebb and the passage fordable at low water (I.3 ¶47). *(Drafted.)*
He says three hours will bring the ebb and the crossing (I.3 ¶58). *(Drafted.)*
He proposes to proceed by method: shelter, fire and food (I.4 ¶5). *(Drafted.)*
He had noticed a narrow cleft a few hundred paces down the coast, which he judged the outlet of a stream (I.4 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He recognises several skuas among the birds on the cliff, and small voracious mews (I.4 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
He takes the lithodomes for mussels, and eats them on Harbert's word (I.4 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
He sees that the Chimneys could be made habitable (I.4 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*
He proposes a log raft to carry the firewood down the river on the ebb (I.4 ¶35). *(Drafted.)*
He makes the raft, binding logs with dry creepers, in an hour (I.4 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
He braids a long rope of dry creepers and tows the raft down on the ebb by hand while Harbert poles it (I.4 ¶63). *(Drafted.)*
He thanks Providence for the fertile land (I.4 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
His first care is to make the Chimneys habitable by stopping the draughty corridors with sand, stones, branches and wet earth (I.5 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*
He lost his pipe too in the shaking (I.5 ¶24). *(Drafted.)*
He searches the shore, river bank and plateau in vain for the box (I.5 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
He asks the reporter and Nab, in the most natural tone, for a match (I.5 ¶55). *(Drafted.)*
Too moved to strike the one match, he hands it to Harbert (I.5 ¶77). *(Drafted.)*
At the fire he says he was never so moved in his life (I.5 ¶80). *(Drafted.)*
He watches near the hearth the whole first night and feeds it generously (I.5 ¶89). *(Drafted.)*
He makes two cudgels from two stout branches broken from the first tree of the forest; Harbert wears the points on a rock (I.6 ¶18). *(Drafted.)*
He searches in vain for palms, which serve so many uses of household life (I.6 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
He makes bird lines of thin lianas knotted together, fifteen to twenty feet long, with strong acacia thorns for hooks and fat red worms for bait, and spares the nests (I.6 ¶41). *(Drafted.)*
He strikes ("ferre") the line with a sharp jerk when three tétras have swallowed bait and hook, and takes them (I.6 ¶47). *(Drafted.)*
He is convinced that Cyrus Smith has drowned (I.7 ¶19). *(Drafted.)*
He feels that Top's coming may give the lie to his conjectures (I.7 ¶68). *(Drafted.)*
He had forgotten to bring the burnt linen, which he could have lit by striking two stones (I.8 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
With Nab and Harbert, and no tools but their arms, he strips a stunted maritime pine of its branches and makes a litter of them, covered with leaves and grass (I.8 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
He rubs two pieces of dry wood together with Nab for an hour, without result (I.9 ¶23). *(Drafted.)*
He makes a log raft at the river's bend, as the first time, and sends the wood down by the current (I.9 ¶118). *(Drafted.)*
He asks Cyrus where they are to begin (I.13 ¶1). *(Drafted.)*
He asks what the kiln will be for (I.13 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
He cries that with only a knife he would soon make a bow and arrows, and game would abound (I.13 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*
He answers Cyrus's two knives with two hurrahs (I.13 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
He gets bows of good strength from crejimba branches strung with hibiscus fibre (I.13 ¶30). *(Drafted.)*
He has some dozens of arrows tipped with porcupine quills that Top retrieved (I.13 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
He clamours for guns (I.13 ¶39). *(Drafted.)*
He helps Nab haul limestone for lime (I.13 ¶44). *(Drafted.)*
He is almost ready to believe the kiln will turn out every product of modern industry (I.13 ¶46). *(Drafted.)*
He makes himself some rough pipes from the clay and finds them charming (I.13 ¶48). *(Drafted.)*
He keeps saying that tobacco will come like all things, in his surges of absolute confidence (I.13 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
He asks, on seeing the mugwort, whether it is tobacco (I.13 ¶54). *(Drafted.)*
He stands aside with the others in Nemo's salon (III.16 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
He and Nab had expected to find almost a god in the "génie de l’île" (III.16 ¶10). *(Drafted.)*
He continues energetic operations; the victory at Petersburg was very dearly contested and his forces, joined with Butler's, still get no result before Richmond (I.2 ¶17). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff searched all over it in vain for his matchbox, in the tall grass on the forest edge (I.5 ¶36). *(Drafted.)*
Smith and Spilett were to spend a day at the Chimneys to examine the shore and the upper plateau (I.9 ¶79). *(Drafted.)*
Smith chose it for his night observation, reserving the right to correct for its height above sea level (I.13 ¶71). *(Drafted.)*
He meant to measure that height next day by simple elementary geometry (I.13 ¶71). *(Drafted.)*
The plateau's height above the sea is to be measured but no figure is given in these chapters.
Nemo threw Top back out of the waters of the lake (III.16 ¶65). *(Drafted.)*
The text gives the lake no size.
At about four o'clock the land was thirty miles to leeward (I.1 ¶57). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
Half an hour later it was one mile away (I.1 ¶60). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
The balloon was two cable-lengths off when it made its last leap (I.1 ¶61). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
The balloon fell on the sand of the shore, beyond the reach of the waves (I.1 ¶61). *(My reading, to confirm.)*
Smith wants to know its distance from America, Australia and the main Pacific archipelagos (I.13 ¶65). *(Drafted.)*
Smith's latitude and longitude workings were put off to the next day and are not given (I.13 ¶78). *(Drafted.)*
The island's latitude and longitude are not given in these chapters.
Pencroff reckoned that a river was needed nearby for drinking water (I.4 ¶8). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff saw in the flow and ebb a way to carry heavy objects (I.4 ¶28). *(Drafted.)*
Smith drank a little of its fresh water, drawn in a large shell (I.9 ¶52). *(Drafted.)*
A raft of logs followed its current back toward the Chimneys (I.9 ¶118). *(Drafted.)*
Nemo sent the boat back into the current of the Mercy (III.16 ¶65). *(Drafted.)*
Nab swam it slantwise in more than half an hour and came ashore several thousand feet from the point opposite where he started (I.3 ¶49). *(Drafted.)*
Spilett, Harbert and Pencroff waded it at about ten o'clock on 25 March, clothes bundled on their heads; Harbert swam (I.3 ¶60). *(Drafted.)*

Spilett slept at the back of a dark corridor, Harbert slept, Pencroff watched by the fire, and Nab slept outside on the shore on the first night (I.5 ¶90). *(Drafted.)*

After the storm of the day before, considerable landslips had occurred and big blocks of rock lay on the strand (I.8 ¶90). *(Drafted.)*
In front of the opening the ground was deeply gullied, having suffered a violent assault of the waves (I.8 ¶91). *(Drafted.)*
The sea had entered to the bottom of the corridors and upset and destroyed everything inside (I.8 ¶94). *(Drafted.)*
The colonists went back to the Chimneys for good on the evening of 15 April (I.13 ¶51). *(Drafted.)*
Nemo brought the dog back to the Chimneys (III.16 ¶65). *(Drafted.)*
In the gale great eddies whirled between the river mouth and the cut face of the wall (I.7 ¶27). *(Drafted.)*
Stones torn from the top of the plateau by the wind's eddies fell on the strand (I.7 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*

After the storm the sea had reached the foot of the enormous granite curtain (I.8 ¶90). *(Drafted.)*
The card does not join this line of reefs to the lines of breakers and reefs on the right of the river mouth in [the bay](the-bay.md); the text does not say whether they are the same.
Pencroff had said that with a knife he would soon make a bow (I.13 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff regrets having forgotten to bring it on the search, for he could easily have lit it by striking two pebbles (I.8 ¶38). *(Drafted.)*
The tools are all they have: Pencroff longs for a knife (I.6 ¶18). *(Drafted.)*
Swung like a scythe, the sticks mowed down whole rows of couroucous (I.6 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
Nab's stick killed the capybara dragged to the bank (I.9 ¶114). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff kept the fire up through the first night without sparing it (I.5 ¶89). *(Drafted.)*
Harbert threw an armful of dry wood onto the hearth (I.7 ¶20). *(Drafted.)*
Nab, Harbert and Pencroff were to go back to the forest to renew the stock of wood (I.9 ¶79). *(Drafted.)*
Smith had saluted it a few days before at the top of Mount Franklin (I.13 ¶58). *(Drafted.)*
Spilett holds a notebook in one hand and a revolver in the other in battle (I.2 ¶9). *(Drafted.)*
His last words noted in it before capture were "Un sudiste me couche en joue et…" (I.2 ¶11). *(Drafted.)*
Pencroff fears Spilett would rather have kept his notebook than his matchbox (I.5 ¶33). *(Drafted.)*
